Rethinking Epistemic Uncertainty in Node Classification through Information Growth

Emma Meneghini Affiliation: University of Trento Affiliation: Fondazione Bruno Kessler, FBK    Francesco Ferrini Affiliation: Fondazione Bruno Kessler, FBK    Bruno Lepri Affiliation: Fondazione Bruno Kessler, FBK    Andrea Passerini Affiliation: University of Trento    Veronica Lachi Affiliation: University of Tromsø
Abstract

Epistemic uncertainty should decrease as additional information about the data-generating process (DGP) becomes available to the predictor. Yet, existing graph evidential deep learning (EDL) methods for node classification typically construct epistemic uncertainty from graph-specific properties and evaluate it on downstream tasks such as out-of-distribution detection, which do not test its reducibility as information about the DGP increases. To make reducibility directly testable, we introduce a statistical framework for studying epistemic uncertainty under information growth. Our framework specifies an information-growth experimental protocol and a consistency criterion for epistemic predictors, while using projective graph DGPs to ensure that growing graphs, which in general need not provide increasing information about the same DGP, constitute coherent observations of the same underlying process. We show that EDL methods do not explicitly estimate data uncertainty arising from a single finite graph observation and instead regulate epistemic uncertainty through model hyperparameters, precluding consistency, as corroborated by controlled information-growth experiments. As an alternative, we propose graph bootstrap ensembles, capturing both data and procedural uncertainty through graph resampling and randomized training. Under the same experimental protocol, these ensembles exhibit epistemic uncertainty reduction beyond standard deep ensembles. These findings support bootstrap ensembles as candidate consistent epistemic predictors under information growth.

1 Introduction

Machine learning models are increasingly expected to provide not only accurate predictions, but also reliable estimates of predictive uncertainty (Abdar et al., 2021; Gawlikowski et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2025). Predictive uncertainty is commonly decomposed into aleatoric uncertainty, arising from intrinsic ambiguity in the data-generating process (DGP) and thus irreducible, and epistemic uncertainty, arising from limited knowledge of that process and thus reducible with additional data (Hüllermeier and Waegeman, 2021; Sale et al., 2026). In classical supervised learning with independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) observations, under suitable regularity conditions, epistemic uncertainty is operationally characterized to decrease monotonically as information increases and eventually vanish (Bengs et al., 2022; Juergens et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2024).

Extending this characterization to node classification on graphs is non-trivial. While increasing sample size provides a natural information-growth mechanism in the i.i.d. setting, no analogous mechanism is readily available for node classification. Intuitively, information growth would involve progressively larger graph observations and training sets becoming available, allowing predictors to be retrained on more informative observations for the same node classification problem. However, nodes are dependent, and observing more of them does not necessarily yield more information about the same underlying DGP (Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013). Consequently, node classification currently lacks a framework for assessing the reducibility of epistemic uncertainty under information growth.

Graph uncertainty quantification has been studied using a variety of approaches (see Wang et al. (2024); Chen et al. (2024) for reviews). Among these, evidential deep learning (EDL) methods (Zhao et al., 2020; Stadler et al., 2021; Hart et al., 2023; Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024b; Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024a) are particularly relevant because they make the epistemic interpretation a central modeling objective, prescribing appropriate uncertainty behavior through graph-specific principles, including reducibility through feature support and structural support, and the reducibility or irreducibility due to neighborhood conflict. However, these principles are defined with respect to the features and topology of a fixed observed graph rather than under information growth. Empirical evaluations likewise assess epistemic uncertainty through its utility for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, whose optimal predictors need not coincide with predictors of reducible epistemic uncertainty (Paplhám et al., 2026). While informative about task-specific downstream utility, such evaluations therefore cannot establish whether an uncertainty score has this epistemic interpretation.

Together, these limitations raise fundamental questions about how epistemic uncertainty should be defined and modeled in node classification. We investigate these issues through three research questions: (RQ1) What constitutes a principled statistical framework for epistemic predictors in node classification? (RQ2) Are graph EDL models consistent epistemic predictors, and, if not, what are their fundamental limitations? (RQ3) Which alternative approach can address these limitations?

Contributions. We address these questions through three main contributions.

(1) We establish the first statistical framework for epistemic uncertainty under information growth in node classification, comprising an information-growth experimental protocol and a definition of consistent epistemic predictors. The former naturally requires projective graph DGPs to preserve the underlying node-classification problem across nested graphs and learning tasks (Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013), while the latter requires decreasing and asymptotically vanishing uncertainty. Together, these provide a statistical basis for assessing epistemic reducibility beyond conventional evaluations.

(2) We unify graph EDL objectives and characterize their population optima, showing how model hyperparameters artificially regulate epistemic uncertainty in the absence of explicit estimation of data uncertainty (Shen et al., 2024), arising from observing a single finite realization of the DGP, ultimately precluding epistemic consistency. Controlled information-growth experiments on projective graphs confirm insufficient epistemic concentration and persistent parameterization dependence, corroborating the structural limitations that undermine their use as consistent epistemic predictors.

(3) Motivated by evidence that bootstrap-based ensembles capture data and procedural uncertainty (Jimenez et al., 2026), thus enabling decreasing epistemic uncertainty in the i.i.d. setting (Jain and Bates, 2025), we extend this approach to graphs through graph bootstrap ensembles. Under the same protocol as in (2), the experiments support these ensembles as a family of candidate consistent epistemic predictors, demonstrating the ability to recover epistemic concentration absent from standard deep ensembles.

Together, these contributions establish a statistical foundation for understanding epistemic uncertainty in node classification, reveal the limitations of existing evidential approaches when assessed through information growth, and introduce graph bootstrap ensembles as a theoretically motivated, empirically supported alternative for modeling epistemic uncertainty that contracts under information growth.

2 Background on Predictive Uncertainty and Motivation

Let 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ){\mathcal{G}}=({\mathcal{V}},{\mathcal{E}}) be an undirected attributed graph with |𝒱|=N|{\mathcal{V}}|=N, adjacency matrix A∈{0,1}N×NA\in\{0,1\}^{N\times N}, and node feature matrix X∈ℝN×DX\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}. Let 𝒴={1,…,C}{\mathcal{Y}}=\{1,\ldots,C\} denote the set of class labels. In semi-supervised node classification, a set of labeled nodes 𝒯(tr)⊂𝒱{\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}\subset{\mathcal{V}} is used to predict the labels of the remaining nodes 𝒯(te)=𝒱∖𝒯(tr){\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{te})}={\mathcal{V}}\setminus{\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}. We consider quantifying the uncertainty of these predictions. A probabilistic classifier associates each node i∈𝒱i\in{\mathcal{V}} with a predictive categorical distribution θ(i)∈ΔC\theta^{(i)}\in\Delta_{C}, where ΔC={θ∈ℝC:θc≥0,∑c=1Cθc=1}\Delta_{C}=\{\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{C}:\theta_{c}\geq 0,\;\sum_{c=1}^{C}\theta_{c}=1\} denotes the probability simplex over 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}}. We adopt a second-order probabilistic framework in which the predictive distribution is itself regarded as a random variable Θ(i)\Theta^{(i)}. The second-order predictor Q(i)Q^{(i)} specifies a distribution over predictive distributions Θ(i)∼Q(i)\Theta^{(i)}\sim Q^{(i)}, with Q:(𝒢,i)↦𝒫⁡(ΔC)Q:({\mathcal{G}},i)\mapsto{\mathcal{P}}(\Delta_{C}). We use the standard information-theoretic decomposition of total predictive uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic components (Depeweg, 2019; Wimmer et al., 2023). Since the following quantities are defined node-wise, we omit the superscript (i) and define the predictive mean by θ¯=𝔼Q​[Θ]\bar{\theta}=\mathbb{E}_{Q}[\Theta]. The total uncertainty (TU) is the Shannon entropy of the predictive mean,

TU(Q)=H(𝔼Q[Θ])=−∑c=1Cθ¯clogθ¯c.\mathrm{TU}(Q)=H(\mathbb{E}_{Q}[\Theta])=-\sum_{c=1}^{C}\bar{\theta}_{c}\log\bar{\theta}_{c}. (1)

Aleatoric uncertainty (AU) is the irreducible uncertainty about the class label remaining after conditioning on the predictive distribution and is given by the conditional entropy H⁡(Y|Θ)H(Y|\Theta),

AU(Q)=H(Y|Θ)=𝔼Q[H(θ)]=−∫ΔC∑c=1CθclogθcdQ(θ).\mathrm{AU}(Q)=H(Y|\Theta)=\mathbb{E}_{Q}[H(\theta)]=-\int_{\Delta_{C}}\sum_{c=1}^{C}\theta_{c}\log\theta_{c}\,dQ(\theta). (2)

Epistemic uncertainty (EU) quantifies uncertainty about which predictive distribution should be assigned to the node and is given by the mutual information (MI) II between YY and Θ\Theta,

EU(Q)=I(Y;Θ)=TU(Q)−AU(Q)=𝔼Q[DKL(θ∥θ¯)],\mathrm{EU}(Q)=I(Y;\Theta)=\mathrm{TU}(Q)-\mathrm{AU}(Q)=\mathbb{E}_{Q}\left[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\theta\|\bar{\theta})\right], (3)

where DKL(⋅∥⋅)D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\cdot\|\cdot) denotes the Kullback-Leibler divergence. We next review graph EDL methods, which directly parameterize QQ and are the main second-order baselines considered in this work.

2.1 Graph EDL Models

Evidential node classifiers predict a second-order Dirichlet distribution Qψ(i)=Dir⁡(θ,α(i))Q_{\psi}^{(i)}=\mathrm{Dir}(\theta;\alpha^{(i)}), with α(i)=𝟏+e(i)\alpha^{(i)}=\mathbf{1}+e^{(i)} and class-wise evidence e(i)∈ℝ>0Ce^{(i)}\in\mathbb{R}^{C}_{>0}. Its mean θ¯(i)=α(i)/α0(i)\bar{\theta}^{(i)}=\alpha^{(i)}/\alpha_{0}^{(i)} gives the predictive probabilities, while α0(i)=∑c=1Cαc(i)\alpha_{0}^{(i)}=\sum_{c=1}^{C}\alpha_{c}^{(i)} controls concentration. We organize graph EDL methods by their evidence parameterization and treatment of epistemic uncertainty: reduction through feature support and structural support, and reduction or irreducibility due to neighborhood conflict.

Direct parameterization. S-BGCN-K (Zhao et al., 2020) directly predicts Dirichlet evidence with a Bayesian GNN and uses dropout-induced variability for uncertainty estimation. During training, its prediction is regularized toward a node-specific, graph-dependent GKDE prior assigning higher evidence to nodes closer to labeled nodes of the corresponding class, thereby encoding structural support; S-BGCN-T-K additionally introduces a teacher network to improve predictive performance. Assuming the Gaussian likelihood and denoting the one-hot ground-truth label ey(i)e_{y}^{(i)}, its objective is

ℓMSE(ψ;i)=𝔼θ(i)∼Qψ(i)[∥θ(i)−ey(i)∥2]+λDKL(Qψ(i)∥QGKDEprior,(i)).\ell_{\mathrm{MSE}}(\psi;i)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{(i)}\sim Q_{\psi}^{(i)}}\!\left[\|\theta^{(i)}-e_{y}^{(i)}\|^{2}\right]+\lambda D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\psi}^{(i)}\|Q_{\mathrm{GKDE}}^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}). (4)

Density parameterization. GPN (Stadler et al., 2021) constructs evidence pseudo-counts from class-conditional densities in latent space, so that low-density regions receive little evidence, implementing feature support (Charpentier et al., 2020; Charpentier et al., 2022). These pseudo-counts are propagated through Personalized PageRank, βcagg,(i)=∑j∈𝒱Πi,jPPR​βcft,(j)\beta_{c}^{\mathrm{agg},(i)}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{V}}}\Pi^{\mathrm{PPR}}_{i,j}\beta_{c}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}, yielding α(i)=𝟏+βagg,(i)\alpha^{(i)}=\mathbf{1}+\beta^{\mathrm{agg},(i)}, where 𝟏\mathbf{1} is a uniform Dirichlet prior. Propagation implements structural support by diffusing evidence across neighboring nodes, while accumulating conflicting class evidence within the same Dirichlet implements neighborhood conflict, attributing disagreement to irreducible aleatoric uncertainty. Assuming the categorical likelihood p⁡(y(i)|θ(i))=θy(i)p(y^{(i)}|\theta^{(i)})=\theta_{y^{(i)}}, GPN minimizes

ℓUCE​(ψ,i)=𝔼θ(i)∼Qψ(i)​[−ey(i)⊤​log⁡θ(i)]−λ​H​[Qψ(i)].\ell_{\mathrm{UCE}}(\psi;i)=\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{(i)}\sim Q_{\psi}^{(i)}}[-e_{y}^{(i)\top}\log\theta^{(i)}]-\lambda H[Q_{\psi}^{(i)}]. (5)

Distance-regularized GPN-GD (Hart et al., 2023) augments this formulation with pairwise regularization of latent representations and evidence.

CUQ-GNN (Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024a) retains the density-based parameterization and UCE objective but replaces the independent encoder and subsequent propagation step with a GNN encoder, jointly learning feature support, structural support, and the handling of neighborhood conflict. GPN-LOP (Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024b) instead retains GPN’s feature pseudo-counts but aggregates the resulting Dirichlet distributions, Qψ(i)=∑j∈𝒱Πi,jPPR​Qψft,(j)Q_{\psi}^{(i)}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{V}}}\Pi^{\mathrm{PPR}}_{i,j}Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}, allowing neighborhood disagreement to contribute to epistemic, rather than necessarily aleatoric, uncertainty. It is trained using a tractable upper bound on the UCE loss of the mixture,

ℓGPN−LOP​(ψ,i)=∑j∈𝒱Πi,jPPR​(𝔼θ(j)∼Qψft,(j)​[−ey(i)⊤​log⁡θ(j)]−λ​H​[Qψft,(j)]).\ell_{\mathrm{GPN-LOP}}(\psi;i)=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{V}}}\Pi^{\mathrm{PPR}}_{i,j}\left(\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{(j)}\sim Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}}[-e_{y}^{(i)\top}\log\theta^{(j)}]-\lambda H[Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}]\right). (6)

2.2 Why Evaluate Epistemic Uncertainty under Information Growth?

Epistemic uncertainty is commonly considered useful a priori for downstream tasks such as OOD detection on graphs, as the lack of model knowledge about OOD inputs is expected to result in higher epistemic uncertainty (Bazhenov et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024), and performance on these benchmarks is therefore used to assess the quality of EDL uncertainty estimates. However, our results show that the most effective uncertainty type depends on the particular model and OOD protocol, with AU/TU typically performing best for leave-out-classes (LOC) and feature isolation (FI) with Bernoulli perturbations, and EU for Gaussian FI (Table 1; additional results in Appendix F). That non-epistemic components can outperform EU supports growing criticism that OOD discrimination and the reducibility of epistemic uncertainty under increasing information constitute distinct objectives whose optimal predictors need not coincide (Li et al., 2025; Paplhám et al., 2026). This motivates evaluating epistemic uncertainty under information growth.

3 A Statistical Framework for Graph Epistemic Uncertainty

Addressing (RQ1), we extend the i.i.d. characterization of epistemic predictors (Bengs et al., 2022; Juergens et al., 2024) to node classification by defining a statistical framework with an information-growth experimental protocol and a consistency criterion for epistemic predictors.

3.1 Information-Growth Experimental Protocol

Constructing an information-growth experimental protocol for node classification requires three components: (i) the sampling unit, i.e., what constitutes one observation from the DGP; (ii) the sampling scheme, i.e., how increasingly informative observations are generated from the same DGP; and (iii) the learning task, i.e., how the supervised prediction problem evolves along this sequence.

Sampling unit. Unlike classical datasets, the nodes of a graph are not a collection of i.i.d. observations. We therefore take the observed graph 𝒢=(𝒱,ℰ){\mathcal{G}}=({\mathcal{V}},{\mathcal{E}}), equivalently the subgraph induced by 𝒱{\mathcal{V}}, as the sampling unit, following the graph-as-observation perspective of Shalizi and Rinaldo (2013). Increasing information then corresponds to observing nested graphs 𝒢⊂𝒢′{\mathcal{G}}\subset{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}, with 𝒱⊂𝒱′{\mathcal{V}}\subset{\mathcal{V}}^{\prime} and 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} equal to the subgraph of 𝒢′{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime} induced by 𝒱{\mathcal{V}}.

Sampling scheme. Requiring two nested graphs to arise from the same DGP is non-trivial. This consistency is implicit in the i.i.d. setting, where every finite sample is a restriction of the same infinite sequence, but need not hold across graphs of different sizes. We make it explicit through projectibility (Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013). Let 𝒜{\mathcal{A}} be a collection of finite subsets of a countable node index set 𝕀\mathbb{I}, ordered by inclusion, and let {ℙA,ϕ}A∈𝒜,ϕ∈Φ\{\mathbb{P}_{A,\phi}\}_{A\in{\mathcal{A}},\phi\in\Phi} denote a family of finite-dimensional DGPs, where GA∼ℙA,ϕG_{A}\sim\mathbb{P}_{A,\phi} denotes the attributed graph indexed by AA. For A⊂BA\subset B, let πB→A\pi_{B\to A} denote the natural projection that restricts an observation indexed by BB to the indices in AA.

Definition 3.1 (Projective DGP).

The family {ℙA,ϕ}A∈𝒜,ϕ∈Φ\{\mathbb{P}_{A,\phi}\}_{A\in{\mathcal{A}},\phi\in\Phi} is projective if, for every A⊂BA\subset B,

ℙA,ϕ=ℙB,ϕ∘πB→A−1∀ϕ∈Φ.\mathbb{P}_{A,\phi}=\mathbb{P}_{B,\phi}\circ\pi^{-1}_{B\to A}\qquad\forall\phi\in\Phi. (7)

Thus, projectibility gives a coherent meaning to information growth by ensuring that every smaller observation has exactly the distribution obtained by marginalizing any larger observation under the stochastic process with the same parameter ϕ\phi. Moreover, by the Kolmogorov extension theorem (Kallenberg, 1997), every such projective family uniquely defines an infinite-dimensional distribution ℙϕ\mathbb{P}_{\phi} whose finite-dimensional marginals are precisely {ℙA,ϕ}A∈𝒜\{\mathbb{P}_{A,\phi}\}_{A\in{\mathcal{A}}}. Dense graphons are an important class of projective graph families (Veitch and Roy, 2015) and will serve as the concrete instantiation of this framework in our experiments. Other prominent graph models, including many exponential random graph models and sparse random graph formulations, are not projective (Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013; Schweinberger et al., 2017).

Learning task. Finally, the supervised tasks induced by increasingly large graph observations must exploit the corresponding information growth. If 𝒯(tr)⊂𝒱{\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}\subset{\mathcal{V}} and 𝒯′(tr)⊂𝒱′{\mathcal{T}}^{\prime(\mathrm{tr})}\subset{\mathcal{V}}^{\prime} denote the training sets associated with 𝒢⊂𝒢′{\mathcal{G}}\subset{\mathcal{G}}^{\prime}, respectively, we require 𝒯(tr)⊂𝒯′(tr){\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}\subset{\mathcal{T}}^{\prime(\mathrm{tr})}, so that each larger task extends the previous one with additional information about the same underlying node-classification problem. Validation and test sets are defined analogously.

3.2 Consistent Epistemic Predictors

We now characterize a consistent epistemic predictor under this information-growth experimental protocol. For an increasing sequence An⊂An+1A_{n}\subset A_{n+1}, with |An|=n|A_{n}|=n, let QAn={QAn(i)}i∈AnQ_{A_{n}}=\{Q_{A_{n}}^{(i)}\}_{i\in A_{n}} denote the collection of node-wise second-order predictors. For an epistemic uncertainty measure UU, we define the uncertainty of this collection as the average node-wise uncertainty U¯An:=|An|−1​∑i∈AnU⁡(QAn(i))\bar{U}_{A_{n}}:=|A_{n}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in A_{n}}U(Q_{A_{n}}^{(i)}). We define consistency over the full node set 𝒜n{\mathcal{A}}_{n}, even though empirically we evaluate uncertainty on the test nodes. Let pϕ⋆p_{\phi}^{\star} denote the Bayes-optimal predictor under the infinite-dimensional law ℙϕ\mathbb{P}_{\phi} induced by projectibility, and pϕ⋆|Anp_{\phi}^{\star}|A_{n} its restriction to AnA_{n}.

Definition 3.2 (Consistent epistemic predictors).

Under the information-growth experimental protocol defined in Section 3.1, a sequence of collections of second-order predictors {QAn}n≥1\{Q_{A_{n}}\}_{n\geq 1} is consistent if the following two conditions hold:

  1. 1.

    Monotonicity. For every nn, 𝔼GAn​[U¯An]≥𝔼GAn+1​[U¯An+1]\mathbb{E}_{G_{A_{n}}}[\bar{U}_{A_{n}}]\geq\mathbb{E}_{G_{A_{n+1}}}[\bar{U}_{A_{n+1}}]. Furthermore, there exist n0n_{0} and k>0k>0 such that 𝔼GAn0​[U¯An0]>𝔼GAn0+k​[U¯An0+k]\mathbb{E}_{G_{A_{n_{0}}}}[\bar{U}_{A_{n_{0}}}]>\mathbb{E}_{G_{A_{n_{0}+k}}}[\bar{U}_{A_{n_{0}+k}}].

  2. 2.

    Consistency. As |An|→∞|A_{n}|\to\infty, QAnQ_{A_{n}} converges in probability to the Dirac measure at pϕ⋆|Anp_{\phi}^{\star}|A_{n} under the distance d⁡(QAn,δpϕ|An⋆)=|An|−1​∑i∈And⁡(QAn(i),δpϕ|An⋆(i))d(Q_{A_{n}},\delta_{p^{\star}_{\phi|A_{n}}})=|A_{n}|^{-1}\sum_{i\in A_{n}}d(Q_{A_{n}}^{(i)},\delta_{p^{\star}_{\phi|A_{n}}}^{(i)}), where the node-wise distance dd metrizes weak convergence on 𝒫⁡(ΔC){\mathcal{P}}(\Delta_{C}).

These requirements characterize epistemic uncertainty as reducible with information: by condition (1), it decreases in expectation, excluding constant uncertainty sequences (Juergens et al., 2024), and by (2), it vanishes through concentration on the limiting Bayes-optimal predictor (Bengs et al., 2022). For the entropy-based uncertainty considered here, this yields limn→∞𝔼GAn[U¯An)]=0\lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}_{G_{A_{n}}}[\bar{U}_{A_{n}})]=0, leaving only true aleatoric uncertainty. Such consistency requires strong assumptions (Jain and Bates, 2025); in practice, model misspecification and estimation bias may affect the predictor’s estimates without being explicitly represented by its epistemic uncertainty (Jimenez et al., 2026).

4 Graph EDL under Information Growth

We examine graph EDL methods considered in Section 2.1 when estimation and approximation errors are removed. By analyzing their population optima, we study whether they are consistent epistemic predictors per Definition 3.2. Unlike their i.i.d. counterparts, these methods incorporate graph-specific uncertainty principles and losses, motivating an extension of the analogous population-level analysis by Shen et al. (2024). To analyze them within a common framework, we express their objectives through the following unified loss.

Definition 4.1 (Unified EDL loss).

Let QpriorQ^{\mathrm{prior}} be a fixed Dirichlet prior, p⁡(y|θ)p(y|\theta) a likelihood, and ν>0\nu>0 a tempering parameter. For each node ii, the unified EDL loss is

ℓU(ψ;i):=DKL(Qψ(i)∥Qν(⋅|y(i))),\ell_{\mathrm{U}}(\psi;i):=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\psi}^{(i)}\|Q_{\nu}(\cdot|y^{(i)})), (8)

where Qν​(θ|y)∝Qprior​(θ)​p​(y|θ)νQ_{\nu}(\theta|y)\propto Q^{\mathrm{prior}}(\theta)p(y|\theta)^{\nu} denotes the tempered posterior.

The next lemma establishes the equivalence between ℓU\ell_{\mathrm{U}} and the training objectives of each method.

Lemma 4.2.

The unified EDL loss ℓU\ell_{\mathrm{U}} is equivalent, up to positive scaling and a ψ\psi-independent additive constant, to the EDL objectives under the following choices:

  1. 1.

    p⁡(ey(i)|θ(i))=𝒩⁡(ey(i),θ(i),σ2​IC)p(e_{y}^{(i)}|\theta^{(i)})={\mathcal{N}}(e_{y}^{(i)};\theta^{(i)},\sigma^{2}I_{C}), QpriorQ^{\mathrm{prior}} is a fixed Dirichlet prior, and λ=2​σ2/ν\lambda=2\sigma^{2}/\nu, yielding ℓMSE\ell_{\mathrm{MSE}}.

  2. 2.

    p⁡(y(i)|θ(i))=θy(i)(i)p(y^{(i)}|\theta^{(i)})=\theta_{y^{(i)}}^{(i)}, QpriorQ^{\mathrm{prior}} is a uniform Dirichlet prior, and λ=ν−1\lambda=\nu^{-1}, yielding ℓUCE\ell_{\mathrm{UCE}}.

  3. 3.

    With a uniform Dirichlet prior QpriorQ^{\mathrm{prior}} and λ=ν−1\lambda=\nu^{-1}, evaluating the UCE loss at the PPR-weighted soft target e~y(j)\tilde{e}_{y}^{(j)} yields the reformulated GPN-LOP node-wise objective ℓ~GPN−LOP​(ψ,j)∝ℓ~UCE​(ψ,j)\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{GPN-LOP}}(\psi,j)\propto\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{UCE}}(\psi,j); hence, it is equivalent to the unified objective ℓ~U​(ψ,j)\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{U}}(\psi;j).

We now characterize the population optimum of this common loss.

Theorem 4.3.

The population minimizer of the unified EDL loss ℓU\ell_{\mathrm{U}} under ℙϕ\mathbb{P}_{\phi} satisfies

arg​minψ𝔼ℙϕ​(𝐀,𝐗,Y)[ℓU(ψ;i)]=arg​minψ𝔼ℙϕ​(𝐀,𝐗)[DKL(Qψ(i)∥Q⋆,(i))],\argmin_{\psi}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\phi}({\mathbf{A}},{\mathbf{X}},Y)}[\ell_{\mathrm{U}}(\psi;i)]=\argmin_{\psi}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\phi}({\mathbf{A}},{\mathbf{X}})}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\psi}^{(i)}\|Q^{\star,(i)})], (9)

where

Q⋆,(i)​(θ)=Qprior​(θ)​exp⁡(ν​𝔼ℙϕ​(y(i)|𝐗,𝐀)​[log⁡p⁡(y(i)|θ(i))])∫ΔCQprior​(θ′)​exp⁡(ν​𝔼ℙϕ​(y(i)|𝐗,𝐀)​[log⁡p⁡(y(i)|θ′)])​d​θ′.Q^{\star,(i)}(\theta)=\frac{Q^{\mathrm{prior}}(\theta)\exp(\nu\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\phi}(y^{(i)}|{\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{A}})}[\log p(y^{(i)}|\theta^{(i)})])}{\int_{\Delta_{C}}Q^{\mathrm{prior}}(\theta^{\prime})\exp(\nu\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\phi}(y^{(i)}|{\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{A}})}[\log p(y^{(i)}|\theta^{\prime})])\,d\theta^{\prime}}. (10)

The proofs of Lemma 4.2 and Theorem 4.3 are provided in Appendix A.1. For fixed QpriorQ^{\mathrm{prior}} and finite ν\nu, GPN, GPN-LOP, and CUQ-GNN retain non-vanishing epistemic uncertainty at the population optimum, failing Definition 3.2, while their aleatoric uncertainty depends on ν\nu and may differ from that of the Bayes-optimal predictor; see Appendix A.2.1 for more details on GPN-LOP. For S-BGCN-K, an unbounded increase in local evidence, such as under the dense graphon setting, implies convergence of the population-level GKDE prior and the corresponding population optimum to a Dirac distribution; see Appendix A.2.2. With Monte Carlo dropout, however, epistemic uncertainty need not vanish (Verdoja and Kyrki, 2020). The location of the limiting Dirac also depends on the GKDE construction and need not be Bayes-optimal. Moreover, because they are deterministic models, none of these methods account for epistemic uncertainty induced by data sampling (Shen et al., 2024), which is a recognized source of epistemic uncertainty (Jimenez et al., 2026) and, in our setting, corresponds to randomness from observing a single finite graph. S-BGCN-T-K and GPN-GD additionally regularize class-probability estimation and pairwise relations between training nodes, respectively, without introducing further mechanisms for evidence accumulation under graph growth, and are therefore not analyzed separately.

Thus, the asymptotic behavior of epistemic and aleatoric uncertainty predicted by S-BGCN-K, GPN, GPN-LOP, and CUQ-GNN is determined externally, either by the loss regularization or by the construction of the prior. Graph-specific uncertainty principles defined on a fixed graph therefore do not by themselves guarantee the required information-growth behavior.

5 Graph Bootstrap Ensembles

The previous analysis motivates constructing a second-order predictor whose uncertainty is tied explicitly to the information available about the graph DGP. We pursue this idea through graph bootstrap ensembles (GB-Ens), extending deep ensembles, an already understudied approach in node classification (Vieira et al., 2026), to the largely unexplored setting of graph bootstrapping. For each of BB bootstrap graph realizations, we train SS independently initialized GNNs, mirroring i.i.d. bootstrap ensembles that combine procedural and data variability through resampling (Juergens et al., 2024; Shen et al., 2024; Jain and Bates, 2025; Jimenez et al., 2026). The ability to represent both recognized sources of epistemic uncertainty (Jain and Bates, 2025; Jimenez et al., 2026) provides a key motivation for using bootstrap ensembles rather than alternative second-order predictors, including EDL models and deep ensembles, which may fail to capture one or both sources.

In the i.i.d. setting, bootstrap-based MI has also been shown, under suitable conditions, to converge asymptotically to its Bayesian counterpart (Jain and Bates, 2025), providing theoretical support for bootstrap-based epistemic uncertainty estimation with neural networks. For graphs, however, bootstrap guarantees remain restricted to specific combinations of graph DGPs, bootstrap schemes, and estimation targets (Schmid and Desmarais, 2017; Levin and Levina, 2019; Green and Shalizi, 2022; Lin et al., 2020; Shao and Le, 2024), with no analogous result for MI. Nevertheless, projective synthetic graph DGPs whose sampling process can be accurately approximated by a bootstrap procedure provide a tractable setting for studying whether graph bootstrap ensembles empirically exhibit the consistent information-growth behavior of Definition 3.2, analogous to that established in the i.i.d. setting. GB-Ens is also computationally feasible despite increased total cost, through parallel training and sequential inference; see Appendix G for computational comparisons.

Uncertainty decomposition. For node ii, let θb,s(i)∈ΔC\theta_{b,s}^{(i)}\in\Delta_{C} be the predictive distribution from seed ss on bootstrap realization bb. The resulting second-order predictor and predictive mean are

QB,S(i)=1B​S​∑b=1B∑s=1Sδθb,s(i),θ¯(i)=1B​S​∑b=1B∑s=1Sθb,s(i),Q_{B,S}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{BS}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\delta_{\theta_{b,s}^{(i)}},\qquad\bar{\theta}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{BS}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\theta_{b,s}^{(i)}, (11)

where δθb,s(i)\delta_{\theta_{b,s}^{(i)}} denotes the Dirac measure concentrated at θb,s(i)\theta_{b,s}^{(i)}, with

TU(i)=H⁡(θ¯(i)),AU(i)=1B​S​∑b=1B∑s=1SH⁡(θb,s(i)),EU(i)=TU(i)−AU(i).\mathrm{TU}^{(i)}=H(\bar{\theta}^{(i)}),\qquad\mathrm{AU}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{BS}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\sum_{s=1}^{S}H(\theta_{b,s}^{(i)}),\qquad\mathrm{EU}^{(i)}=\mathrm{TU}^{(i)}-\mathrm{AU}^{(i)}. (12)

The crossed B×SB\times S design further allows us to separate the two sources of epistemic uncertainty represented by GB-Ens. With the seed-averaged prediction θ¯b(i)=S−1​∑s=1Sθb,s(i)\bar{\theta}_{b}^{(i)}=S^{-1}\sum_{s=1}^{S}\theta_{b,s}^{(i)},

EUboot(i)=H⁡(θ¯(i))−1B​∑b=1BH⁡(θ¯b(i)),EUseed(i)=1B​∑b=1B[H⁡(θ¯b(i))−1S​∑s=1SH⁡(θb,s(i))].\mathrm{EU}_{\mathrm{boot}}^{(i)}=H(\bar{\theta}^{(i)})-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}H(\bar{\theta}_{b}^{(i)}),\qquad\mathrm{EU}_{\mathrm{seed}}^{(i)}=\frac{1}{B}\sum_{b=1}^{B}\left[H(\bar{\theta}_{b}^{(i)})-\frac{1}{S}\sum_{s=1}^{S}H(\theta_{b,s}^{(i)})\right]. (13)

Here, EUboot\mathrm{EU}_{\mathrm{boot}} measures disagreement across bootstrap graph realizations, while EUseed\mathrm{EU}_{\mathrm{seed}} measures training-induced disagreement within each realization, and EU(i)=EUboot(i)+EUseed(i)\mathrm{EU}^{(i)}=\mathrm{EU}_{\mathrm{boot}}^{(i)}+\mathrm{EU}_{\mathrm{seed}}^{(i)}.

Graph resampling. To instantiate the graph-resampling component of GB-Ens, we adopt a local non-parametric bootstrap adapted from Jeong and Donnat (2025), developed under an exchangeable graphon model. It estimates asymptotically unbiased edge probabilities from the observed connectivity of similar nodes and samples graph realizations accordingly. We use an edge-only bootstrap that retains node identities, features, and labels across realizations, thereby preserving the node classification task while capturing sampling variability in the graph structure. The complete resampling procedure and implementation details are given in Appendix C.

6 Experiments

We empirically address (RQ2)–(RQ3) through controlled experiments on synthetic projective graph DGPs. For (RQ2), we validate our analysis of graph EDL uncertainty under information growth. For (RQ3), we assess graph bootstrap ensembles as an alternative approach to epistemic prediction. Code is available at https://github.com/emmamenegh/Research-Code-Release.

Models. We evaluate S-BGCN-K and S-BGCN-T-K (Zhao et al., 2020), GPN (Stadler et al., 2021), GPN-GDEVI and GPN-GDLAT (Hart et al., 2023), GPN-LOP (Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024b), CUQ-APPNP, CUQ-GAT, and CUQ-GCN (Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024a) as EDL baselines, and GB-Ens with APPNP, GAT, and GCN architectures. Each GB-Ens comprises 25×425\times 4 models, corresponding to 2525 bootstrap samples and 44 random seeds per sample. Model parameterizations are reported in Appendix D.

Datasets. Our experiments comprise two synthetic projective graphon DGPs. The synthetic DGPs are an exponential-decay graphon and an assortative stochastic-block model (SBM), which define complementary continuous- and discrete-structure regimes for a balanced seven-class node-classification problem. For each DGP, we generate 2020 independent replicates of a projective sequence, with six graph sizes logarithmically spaced between 500500 and 10,00010{,}000 nodes. At each graph size, we use 5%/15%/80%5\%/15\%/80\% class-stratified train/validation/test splits constructed according to the protocol in Section 3.1 and fixed across bootstrap replicates for each observed graph. Full DGP specifications and graphon statistics are reported in Appendices B and C.

RQ2: Graph EDL models are inconsistent epistemic predictors.

We examine whether the uncertainty behavior of graph EDL models characterized at the nonparametric population optimum by Theorem 4.3 persists with finite data and parametric models. We assess both EU concentration with increasing information and the dependence of EU and AU on model parameterization. Figure 1(a) shows mean EU across 2020 projective-sequence replicates of the exponential-decay graphon, with 95%95\% bootstrap confidence intervals (CIs). S-BGCN-K and S-BGCN-T-K exhibit decreasing EU, as permitted by their information-dependent prior, but remain non-negligible over the observed sequence, whereas GPN, GPN-GD, GPN-LOP, and CUQ-GNN remain approximately constant, consistent with their population optima retaining finite evidence. EU magnitude also differs substantially across methods, reflecting its theoretical dependence on the parameterization, as illustrated by the similar magnitudes of GPN, GPN-GD, and CUQ-GNN under shared parameter values. At N=10,000N=10{,}000, varying the EDL regularization parameter λ\lambda reveals substantial changes in AU on the same observed graph (Figure 1(b)), demonstrating its dependence on model parameterization rather than on the DGP alone. Analogous results for the SBM are reported in Appendix E.

RQ3: GB-Ens is a family of candidate consistent epistemic predictors.

Figure 2(a) shows mean GB-Ens epistemic uncertainty across 2020 projective-sequence replicates of the exponential-decay graphon, with pointwise 95%95\% bootstrap CIs. From N=500N=500 to N=10,000N=10{,}000, EU decreases monotonically by 94%94\% for GCN, 91%91\% for APPNP, and 61%61\% for GAT. On the SBM (Appendix E), EU similarly decreases substantially for APPNP and GCN, whereas GAT shows a weaker, non-monotonic reduction due to persistent randomized-training variability, plausibly reflecting its sensitivity to learned attention weights and additional attention dropout. The decomposition in Figure 2(b) further shows comparable randomized-seed and bootstrap contributions to EU that decrease with increasing information, with relative magnitude depending on the backbone and DGP. Finally, Figure 3(b) shows that GB-Ens AU decreases and eventually stabilizes, with all three backbones approaching similar plateaus, consistent with convergence toward a predictor-independent estimate of aleatoric uncertainty. The same behavior is observed for the SBM (Appendix E).

To assess the effect of graph resampling, we compare GB-Ens with standard graph deep ensembles (G-Ens), trained with 1010 different random seeds on the observed graph using the same backbones. Figure 3(a) shows that, on the exponential-decay graphon, G-Ens exhibit no consistent EU contraction, while Figure 3(b) shows strongly backbone-dependent AU trajectories, with GAT trending upward and GCN continuing to decrease. Similar behavior is observed on the SBM (Appendix E). Moreover, the gap between G-Ens EU and the randomized-training component of GB-Ens widens with graph size, as the latter contracts under information growth while the former does not. Graph resampling therefore does not simply add bootstrap variability, but induces convergent behavior also in the seed component, enabling EU contraction that is not observed for standard deep ensembles.

As a simple diagnostic of GB-Ens’s approximation to the full second-order distribution induced by true-DGP resampling, which captures predictive variability without DGP estimation error, we compare the two distributions using normalized node-wise Wasserstein-1 distances. On the exponential-decay graphon, distances remain small and stable with graph size for APPNP (≈0.29\approx 0.29) and GCN (≈0.21\approx 0.21), indicating good agreement, while increasing from 0.450.45 to 0.620.62 for GAT. Similar results on the SBM are reported in Appendix E, suggesting that approximation quality varies across predictors.

Overall, these results support GB-Ens as a family of candidate consistent epistemic predictors. This behavior nevertheless remains predictor-specific, as EU contraction ultimately relies on regularity of the underlying learning procedure; persistent training variability can therefore produce weaker and partly non-monotonic reductions.

7 Conclusions

Take-home message. Epistemic uncertainty in node classification should be assessed through its behavior under increasing information, rather than solely by obeying principles or being useful for downstream tasks on a fixed graph. This perspective identifies consistent epistemic uncertainty as requiring estimates that reflect data uncertainty rather than remaining hyperparameter-dependent, a requirement generally not met by graph EDL models. GB-Ens provides a constructive approach by capturing data and procedural uncertainty, with controlled experiments supporting it as a family of candidate consistent predictors.

Limitations & future work. The theoretical consistency of bootstrap-based graph epistemic predictors remains to be established. Moreover, information-growth behavior cannot be evaluated on standard real-world benchmarks, which lack the sampling process required to generate increasingly informative observations from the same DGP. Benchmarks leveraging real graph-growth mechanisms, where projectibility is often natural (Shalizi and Rinaldo, 2013), could extend our analysis beyond synthetic random graphs, either retaining node classification and motivating improved bootstrap-based predictors or considering tasks more naturally aligned with graph growth.

Appendix A Graph EDL Under Information Growth

A.1 Unified EDL Loss

In this section, we extend the unified formulation of EDL losses from the i.i.d. setting (Shen et al., 2024) to node classification. We begin by defining a unified EDL loss and establishing its equivalence to the MSE and UCE losses used by existing graph EDL methods.

Let QpriorQ^{\mathrm{prior}} be a fixed Dirichlet prior and p⁡(y|θ)p(y|\theta) a likelihood. For a tempering parameter ν>0\nu>0, define the tempered posterior

Qν​(θ|y):=Qprior​(θ)​p​(y|θ)ν∫ΔCQprior​(θ′)​p​(y|θ′)ν​d​θ′.Q_{\nu}(\theta|y):=\frac{Q^{\mathrm{prior}}(\theta)p(y|\theta)^{\nu}}{\int_{\Delta_{C}}Q^{\mathrm{prior}}(\theta^{\prime})p(y|\theta^{\prime})^{\nu}d\theta^{\prime}}. (1)

For each node ii, the unified EDL loss is

ℓU(ψ;i):=DKL(Qψ(i)∥Qν(⋅|y(i))).\ell_{\mathrm{U}}(\psi;i):=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\psi}^{(i)}\|Q_{\nu}(\cdot|y^{(i)})). (2)

Expanding the KL divergence gives

ℓU(ψ;i)=DKL(Qψ(i)∥Qprior)−ν𝔼θ(i)∼Qψ(i)[logp(y(i)|θ(i))]+C,\ell_{\mathrm{U}}(\psi;i)=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\psi}^{(i)}\|Q^{\mathrm{prior}})-\nu\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{(i)}\sim Q_{\psi}^{(i)}}[\log p(y^{(i)}|\theta^{(i)})]+C, (3)

where CC is independent of ψ\psi.

e~y(j):=1wj​∑i∈𝒯(tr)Πi,jPPR​ey(i).\tilde{e}_{y}^{(j)}:=\frac{1}{w_{j}}\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}}\Pi_{i,j}^{\mathrm{PPR}}e_{y}^{(i)}. (10)

The reformulated GPN-LOP node-wise loss satisfies

ℓ~GPN−LOP​(ψ,j)=wj​ℓ~UCE​(ψ,j),\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{GPN-LOP}}(\psi;j)=w_{j}\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{UCE}}(\psi;j), (11)

where

ℓ~UCE​(ψ,j):=𝔼θ(j)∼Qψft,(j)​[−e~y(j)⊤​log⁡θ(j)]−λ​H​(Qψft,(j)).\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{UCE}}(\psi;j):=\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{(j)}\sim Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}}[-\tilde{e}_{y}^{(j)\top}\log\theta^{(j)}]-\lambda H(Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}). (12)

Let

ℓ~U(ψ;j):=DKL(Qψft,(j)∥Q~ν(j)),\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{U}}(\psi;j):=D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}\|\tilde{Q}_{\nu}^{(j)}), (13)

where Q~ν(j)\tilde{Q}_{\nu}^{(j)} denotes the tempered posterior under the soft-target categorical likelihood, p⁡(e~y(j)|θ(j))∝∏c=1C(θc(j))e~y,c(j)p(\tilde{e}_{y}^{(j)}|\theta^{(j)})\propto\prod_{c=1}^{C}(\theta_{c}^{(j)})^{\tilde{e}_{y,c}^{(j)}}. Hence, under this soft-target likelihood, a uniform Dirichlet prior QpriorQ^{\mathrm{prior}}, and λ=ν−1\lambda=\nu^{-1},

ℓ~U​(ψ,j)=νwj​ℓ~GPN−LOP​(ψ,j)+C,\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{U}}(\psi;j)=\frac{\nu}{w_{j}}\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{GPN-LOP}}(\psi;j)+C, (14)

where CC is independent of ψ\psi. Thus, ℓ~GPN−LOP\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{GPN-LOP}} is equivalent, up to scaling and an additive constant, to the unified loss ℓ~U\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{U}} associated with the soft target e~y(j)\tilde{e}_{y}^{(j)}.

Proof.

Starting from the training objective,

ℒ⁡(ψ)=∑i∈𝒯(tr)∑j∈𝒱Πi,jPPR​(𝔼θ(j)∼Qψft,(j)​[−ey(i)⊤​log⁡θ(j)]−λ​H​[Qψft,(j)]),{\mathcal{L}}(\psi)=\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}}\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{V}}}\Pi_{i,j}^{\mathrm{PPR}}\!\left(\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{(j)}\sim Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}}[-e_{y}^{(i)\top}\log\theta^{(j)}]-\lambda H[Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}]\right), (15)

interchanging the finite sums gives

ℒ⁡(ψ)=∑j∈𝒱ℓ~GPN−LOP​(ψ,j).{\mathcal{L}}(\psi)=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{V}}}\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{GPN-LOP}}(\psi;j). (16)

For fixed jj, linearity of expectation yields

ℓ~GPN−LOP​(ψ,j)\displaystyle\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{GPN-LOP}}(\psi;j) =𝔼θ(j)∼Qψft,(j)​[−(∑i∈𝒯(tr)Πi,jPPR​ey(i))⊤​log⁡θ(j)]\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{(j)}\sim Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}}\!\left[-(\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}}\Pi_{i,j}^{\mathrm{PPR}}e_{y}^{(i)})^{\top}\log\theta^{(j)}\right] (17)
−λ∑i∈𝒯(tr)Πi,jPPRH(Qψft,(j))\displaystyle\quad-\lambda\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}}\Pi_{i,j}^{\mathrm{PPR}}H(Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}) (18)
=wj​(𝔼θ(j)∼Qψft,(j)​[−e~y(j)⊤​log⁡θ(j)]−λ​H​(Qψft,(j)))\displaystyle=w_{j}\!\left(\mathbb{E}_{\theta^{(j)}\sim Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)}}[-\tilde{e}_{y}^{(j)\top}\log\theta^{(j)}]-\lambda H(Q_{\psi}^{\mathrm{ft},(j)})\right) (19)
=wj​ℓ~UCE​(ψ,j).\displaystyle=w_{j}\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{UCE}}(\psi;j). (20)

Applying Lemma A.2 to this soft-target extension,

ℓ~U​(ψ,j)=ν​ℓ~UCE​(ψ,j)+C,\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{U}}(\psi;j)=\nu\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{UCE}}(\psi;j)+C, (21)

and substituting ℓ~UCE​(ψ,j)=wj−1​ℓ~GPN−LOP​(ψ,j)\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{UCE}}(\psi;j)=w_{j}^{-1}\tilde{\ell}_{\mathrm{GPN-LOP}}(\psi;j) gives the result. ∎

We next characterize the unconstrained minimizer of the unified objective.

Theorem A.4.

The population minimizer of the unified EDL loss ℓU\ell_{\mathrm{U}} under ℙϕ\mathbb{P}_{\phi} satisfies

arg​minψ𝔼ℙϕ​(𝐗,𝐀,Y)[DKL(Qψ(i)∥Qν(⋅|y(i)))]=arg​minψ𝔼ℙϕ​(𝐀,𝐗)[DKL(Qψ(i)∥Q⋆,(i))],\argmin_{\psi}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\phi}({\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{A}},Y)}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\psi}^{(i)}\|Q_{\nu}(\cdot|y^{(i)}))]=\argmin_{\psi}\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\phi}({\mathbf{A}},{\mathbf{X}})}[D_{\mathrm{KL}}(Q_{\psi}^{(i)}\|Q^{\star,(i)})], (22)

where

Q⋆,(i)​(θ)=Qprior​(θ)​exp⁡(ν​𝔼ℙϕ​(y(i)|𝐗,𝐀)​[log⁡p⁡(y(i)|θ(i))])∫ΔCQprior​(θ′)​exp⁡(ν​𝔼ℙϕ​(y(i)|𝐗,𝐀)​[log⁡p⁡(y(i)|θ′)])​d​θ′.Q^{\star,(i)}(\theta)=\frac{Q^{\mathrm{prior}}(\theta)\exp(\nu\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\phi}(y^{(i)}|{\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{A}})}[\log p(y^{(i)}|\theta^{(i)})])}{\int_{\Delta_{C}}Q^{\mathrm{prior}}(\theta^{\prime})\exp(\nu\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\phi}(y^{(i)}|{\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{A}})}[\log p(y^{(i)}|\theta^{\prime})])\,d\theta^{\prime}}. (23)
Proof.

The proof follows analogously to the i.i.d. case in Theorem 5.1 of Shen et al. (2024), with (𝐀,𝐗)({\mathbf{A}},{\mathbf{X}}) replacing the i.i.d. covariates. ∎

A.2 Model-Specific Population Optima

A.2.1 GPN-LOP

For GPN-LOP, the population-optimal feature-based Dirichlet distribution at node jj is determined by the PPR-weighted conditional class probabilities η~(j)=wj−1​∑k∈𝒯(tr)Πk,jPPR​η(k)\tilde{\eta}^{(j)}=w_{j}^{-1}\sum_{k\in{\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}}\Pi_{k,j}^{\mathrm{PPR}}\eta^{(k)}, where wj=∑k∈𝒯(tr)Πk,jPPRw_{j}=\sum_{k\in{\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{tr})}}\Pi_{k,j}^{\mathrm{PPR}} and η(k)=𝔼ℙϕ​(y(k)|𝐀,𝐗)​[ey(k)]\eta^{(k)}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\phi}(y^{(k)}|{\mathbf{A}},{\mathbf{X}})}[e_{y}^{(k)}]. Under the categorical likelihood and uniform Dirichlet prior, Theorem A.4 therefore gives Qft⋆,(j)=Dir(θ;αprior+νη~(j))Q^{\mathrm{ft}\star,(j)}=\mathrm{Dir}\!\left(\theta;\alpha^{\mathrm{prior}}+\nu\tilde{\eta}^{(j)}\right). Since ∑c=1Cη~c(j)=1\sum_{c=1}^{C}\tilde{\eta}_{c}^{(j)}=1, each component has total concentration α0prior+ν\alpha_{0}^{\mathrm{prior}}+\nu, which remains finite for fixed ν\nu. GPN-LOP aggregates these feature-based distributions through PPR, Q⋆,(i)=∑j∈𝒱Πi,jPPRQft⋆,(j)Q^{\star,(i)}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{V}}}\Pi_{i,j}^{\mathrm{PPR}}Q^{\mathrm{ft}\star,(j)}. Its epistemic uncertainty decomposes as

EU(Q(i))=∑j∈𝒱Πi,jPPREU(Qft,(j))+∑j∈𝒱Πi,jPPRDKL(θ¯(j)∥θ¯(i)),\mathrm{EU}(Q^{(i)})=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{V}}}\Pi^{\mathrm{PPR}}_{i,j}\mathrm{EU}(Q^{\mathrm{ft},(j)})+\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{V}}}\Pi^{\mathrm{PPR}}_{i,j}D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar{\theta}^{(j)}\|\bar{\theta}^{(i)}), (24)

where θ¯(i)=∑j∈𝒱Πi,jPPR​θ¯(j)\bar{\theta}^{(i)}=\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{V}}}\Pi^{\mathrm{PPR}}_{i,j}\bar{\theta}^{(j)}.

The first term is strictly positive for finite ν\nu, since each Dirichlet component has finite concentration, while the second term is non-negative. Hence, the GPN-LOP population optimum retains strictly positive epistemic uncertainty even when the component means agree.

A.2.2 S-BGCN-K

Theorem A.4 characterizes the population optimum for a fixed prior and therefore does not directly apply to S-BGCN-K, whose GKDE prior depends on the observed graph and training labels. Marginalizing this data-dependent prior in the population objective yields an effective prior Qnprior,(i)Q_{n}^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}, defined, for the data-dependent GKDE prior QGAnprior,(i)Q_{G_{A_{n}}}^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}, by

Qnprior,(i)​(θ)∝exp⁡(𝔼GAn∼ℙAn,ϕ​[log⁡QGAnprior,(i)​(θ)]).Q_{n}^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}(\theta)\propto\exp(\mathbb{E}_{G_{A_{n}}\sim\mathbb{P}_{A_{n},\phi}}[\log Q_{G_{A_{n}}}^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}(\theta)]). (25)

This effective prior changes with graph size nn. We first show that convergence of these priors implies convergence of the corresponding population optima, and then establish conditions under which the effective GKDE prior concentrates under graph growth.

Lemma A.5 (Population optima under convergent priors).

Let {Qnprior,(i)}n≥1\{Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{{n}}\}_{n\geq 1} be a sequence of priors such that Qnprior,(i)⇒Q∞prior,(i)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}\Rightarrow Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{\infty}. For fixed finite ν\nu, suppose that g(i)g^{(i)} is continuous and strictly positive on ΔC\Delta_{C}. Then, the corresponding population optima

Qn⋆,(i)​(d​θ)=g(i)​(θ)​Qnprior,(i)​(d​θ)∫ΔCg(i)​(ϑ)​Qnprior,(i)​(𝑑ϑ)Q_{n}^{\star,(i)}(d\theta)=\frac{g^{(i)}(\theta)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}(d\theta)}{\int_{\Delta_{C}}g^{(i)}(\vartheta)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}(d\vartheta)} (26)

satisfy Qn⋆,(i)⇒Q∞⋆,(i)Q_{n}^{\star,(i)}\Rightarrow Q_{\infty}^{\star,(i)}, where Q∞⋆,(i)Q_{\infty}^{\star,(i)} is the population optimum of Theorem A.4 associated with the limiting prior Q∞prior,(i)Q_{\infty}^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}, namely,

Q∞⋆,(i)​(d​θ)=g(i)​(θ)​Q∞prior,(i)​(d​θ)∫ΔCg(i)​(ϑ)​Q∞prior,(i)​(𝑑ϑ).Q_{\infty}^{\star,(i)}(d\theta)=\frac{g^{(i)}(\theta)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{\infty}(d\theta)}{\int_{\Delta_{C}}g^{(i)}(\vartheta)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{\infty}(d\vartheta)}. (27)

Moreover, Q∞⋆,(i)Q_{\infty}^{\star,(i)} is a Dirac distribution if and only if Q∞prior,(i)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{\infty} is a Dirac distribution.

Proof.

For any bounded continuous f:ΔC→ℝf:\Delta_{C}\to\mathbb{R},

∫ΔCf⁡(θ)​Qn⋆,(i)​(𝑑θ)=∫ΔCf⁡(θ)​g(i)​(θ)​Qnprior,(i)​(𝑑θ)∫ΔCg(i)​(θ)​Qnprior,(i)​(𝑑θ).\int_{\Delta_{C}}f(\theta)Q_{n}^{\star,(i)}(d\theta)=\frac{\int_{\Delta_{C}}f(\theta)g^{(i)}(\theta)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}(d\theta)}{\int_{\Delta_{C}}g^{(i)}(\theta)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}(d\theta)}. (28)

Since ΔC\Delta_{C} is compact, continuity of g(i)g^{(i)} implies that g(i)g^{(i)} and f​g(i)fg^{(i)} are bounded and continuous. The assumed weak convergence Qnprior,(i)⇒Q∞prior,(i)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}\Rightarrow Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{\infty} therefore gives

∫f​g(i)​d​Qnprior,(i)→∫f​g(i)​d​Q∞prior,(i)and∫g(i)​d​Qnprior,(i)→∫g(i)​d​Q∞prior,(i).\int fg^{(i)}dQ^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}\to\int fg^{(i)}dQ^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{\infty}\quad\text{and}\quad\int g^{(i)}dQ^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}\to\int g^{(i)}dQ^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{\infty}. (29)

Since g(i)g^{(i)} is strictly positive on ΔC\Delta_{C}, the latter limit is strictly positive, and hence Qn⋆,(i)⇒Q∞⋆,(i)Q_{n}^{\star,(i)}\Rightarrow Q_{\infty}^{\star,(i)}. Moreover, strict positivity implies that Q∞⋆,(i)Q_{\infty}^{\star,(i)} and Q∞prior,(i)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{\infty} have the same null sets, and hence one is concentrated at a single point if and only if the other is. ∎

For the Gaussian likelihood underlying ℓMSE\ell_{\mathrm{MSE}}, we define the likelihood-derived weighting function g(i)​(θ)=exp⁡{ν​𝔼ℙϕ​(y(i)|𝐗,𝐀)​[log⁡p⁡(y(i)|θ)]}g^{(i)}(\theta)=\exp\{\nu\,\mathbb{E}_{\mathbb{P}_{\phi}(y^{(i)}|{\mathbf{X}},{\mathbf{A}})}[\log p(y^{(i)}|\theta)]\}, which is continuous and strictly positive on the compact simplex. Hence, Lemma A.5 applies to any convergent sequence of priors. We next give sufficient conditions for a sequence of Dirichlet priors to concentrate.

Lemma A.6 (Concentration of Dirichlet priors).

Let

Qnprior,(i)=Dir⁡(θ,βn(i)),β0,n(i)=∑c=1Cβn,c(i),mn(i)=βn(i)β0,n(i).Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}=\mathrm{Dir}(\theta;\beta_{n}^{(i)}),\qquad\beta_{0,n}^{(i)}=\sum_{c=1}^{C}\beta_{n,c}^{(i)},\qquad m_{n}^{(i)}=\frac{\beta_{n}^{(i)}}{\beta_{0,n}^{(i)}}. (30)

If β0,n(i)→∞\beta_{0,n}^{(i)}\to\infty and mn(i)→m(i)∈ΔCm_{n}^{(i)}\to m^{(i)}\in\Delta_{C}, then Qnprior,(i)⇒δm(i)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}\Rightarrow\delta_{m^{(i)}}.

Proof.

Let Θn(i)∼Qnprior,(i)\Theta_{n}^{(i)}\sim Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}. Then, 𝔼⁡[Θn(i)]=mn(i)\mathbb{E}[\Theta_{n}^{(i)}]=m_{n}^{(i)}. Moreover, since mn,c(i)∈[0,1]m_{n,c}^{(i)}\in[0,1], we have mn,c(i)​(1−mn,c(i))≤1/4m_{n,c}^{(i)}(1-m_{n,c}^{(i)})\leq 1/4, and thus, for each class cc,

Var⁡(Θn,c(i))=mn,c(i)​(1−mn,c(i))β0,n(i)+1≤14​(β0,n(i)+1)→0,\mathrm{Var}(\Theta_{n,c}^{(i)})=\frac{m_{n,c}^{(i)}(1-m_{n,c}^{(i)})}{\beta_{0,n}^{(i)}+1}\leq\frac{1}{4(\beta_{0,n}^{(i)}+1)}\to 0, (31)

where the convergence follows from β0,n(i)→∞\beta_{0,n}^{(i)}\to\infty. Therefore, Θn(i)−mn(i)→0\Theta_{n}^{(i)}-m_{n}^{(i)}\to 0 in probability. Since mn(i)→m(i)m_{n}^{(i)}\to m^{(i)}, it follows that Θn(i)→m(i)\Theta_{n}^{(i)}\to m^{(i)} in probability, and hence Qnprior,(i)⇒δm(i)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}\Rightarrow\delta_{m^{(i)}}. ∎

Thus, if β0,n(i)→∞\beta_{0,n}^{(i)}\to\infty and mn(i)→m(i)m_{n}^{(i)}\to m^{(i)}, Lemmas A.6 and A.5 give Qnprior,(i)⇒δm(i)Q_{n}^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}\Rightarrow\delta_{m^{(i)}} and Qn⋆,(i)⇒δm(i)Q_{n}^{\star,(i)}\Rightarrow\delta_{m^{(i)}}. Consequently,

EU⁡(Qn⋆,(i))→0andAU⁡(Qn⋆,(i))→H⁡(m(i)).\mathrm{EU}(Q_{n}^{\star,(i)})\to 0\quad\text{and}\quad\mathrm{AU}(Q_{n}^{\star,(i)})\to H(m^{(i)}). (32)

S-BGCN-K provides a graph-dependent Dirichlet prior through GKDE, with parameters

βn,c(i)=1+∑j∈𝒯n(tr)𝟏{y(j)=c}gσ(di​j),\beta_{n,c}^{(i)}=1+\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{n}^{(\mathrm{tr})}}\mathbf{1}\{y^{(j)}=c\}g_{\sigma}(d_{ij}), (33)

where di​jd_{ij} denotes the graph distance between nodes ii and jj, and gσ​(di​j)g_{\sigma}(d_{ij}) is the Gaussian kernel applied to this distance, with bandwidth σ\sigma. Since the expectation of a Dirichlet log-density differs from the log-density of a Dirichlet distribution with expected parameters only by a θ\theta-independent constant, the effective population prior is

Qnprior,(i)=Dir⁡(θ,βn(i)),βn,c(i)=𝔼GAn∼ℙAn,ϕ​[βn,c(i)].Q_{n}^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}=\mathrm{Dir}(\theta;\beta_{n}^{(i)}),\qquad\beta_{n,c}^{(i)}=\mathbb{E}_{G_{A_{n}}\sim\mathbb{P}_{A_{n},\phi}}[\beta_{n,c}^{(i)}]. (34)

Summing over classes gives the total concentration of the effective prior,

β0,n(i)=C+𝔼GAn∼ℙAn,ϕ​[∑j∈𝒯n(tr)gσ​(di​j)].\beta_{0,n}^{(i)}=C+\mathbb{E}_{G_{A_{n}}\sim\mathbb{P}_{A_{n},\phi}}\!\Bigl[\sum_{j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{n}^{(\mathrm{tr})}}g_{\sigma}(d_{ij})\Bigr]. (35)

Thus, concentration grows with the expected amount of kernel-weighted labeled evidence available around node ii. In particular, for any fixed finite DD,

β0,n(i)≥C+gσ​(D)​𝔼GAn∼ℙAn,ϕ​[|{j∈𝒯n(tr):di​j≤D}|],\beta_{0,n}^{(i)}\geq C+g_{\sigma}(D)\mathbb{E}_{G_{A_{n}}\sim\mathbb{P}_{A_{n},\phi}}[|\{j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{n}^{(\mathrm{tr})}:d_{ij}\leq D\}|], (36)

where we use that the Gaussian kernel is non-increasing in distance. Hence, a sufficient condition for β0,n(i)→∞\beta_{0,n}^{(i)}\to\infty is the existence of a fixed DD such that 𝔼GAn∼ℙAn,ϕ​[|{j∈𝒯n(tr):di​j≤D}|]→∞\mathbb{E}_{G_{A_{n}}\sim\mathbb{P}_{A_{n},\phi}}[|\{j\in{\mathcal{T}}_{n}^{(\mathrm{tr})}:d_{ij}\leq D\}|]\to\infty. Under the dense projective graph DGPs considered in our experiments, positive population normalized degree for node ii, together with a training-label sampling scheme that retains a positive fraction of its neighbors, yields a diverging expected number of labeled one-hop neighbors, so the condition holds with D=1D=1. If, in addition, the normalized GKDE evidence converges, mn(i)→m(i)m_{n}^{(i)}\to m^{(i)}, Lemma A.6 gives Qnprior,(i)⇒δm(i)Q^{\mathrm{prior},(i)}_{n}\Rightarrow\delta_{m^{(i)}} and Lemma A.5 then yields Qn⋆,(i)⇒δm(i)Q_{n}^{\star,(i)}\Rightarrow\delta_{m^{(i)}}.

However, m(i)m^{(i)} is the limiting vector of normalized population-averaged kernel-weighted class evidence induced by the GKDE construction and is not guaranteed to coincide with the Bayes-optimal predictor pϕ⋆,(i)p_{\phi}^{\star,(i)}, as it depends on choices such as the GKDE bandwidth and the graph-distance weighting function. Hence, despite concentration of the evidential distribution, Definition 3.2 need not be satisfied, and AU⁡(Qn⋆,(i))→H⁡(m(i))\mathrm{AU}(Q_{n}^{\star,(i)})\to H(m^{(i)}) need not equal the true aleatoric uncertainty H⁡(pϕ⋆,(i))H(p_{\phi}^{\star,(i)}).

The analysis above considers S-BGCN-K with Monte Carlo (MC) dropout disabled, thereby isolating the uncertainty induced by the evidential objective. When MC dropout with a fixed Bernoulli dropout rate is enabled, as in the original formulation, concentration of the evidential distribution is no longer sufficient for concentration of the resulting predictive distribution: the predictions must additionally become invariant to the dropout mask as information grows. Fixed-rate MC dropout does not in general ensure such concentration, and has been shown to retain predictive variability independently of the amount of observed data in simple settings (Verdoja and Kyrki, 2020).

Appendix B Synthetic Graphons

We consider two complementary homophilic graph DGPs: a smooth exponential-decay graphon, representing continuous latent similarity, and an assortative stochastic block model (SBM) graphon, representing discrete community structure, both commonly considered in the literature (Xu et al., 2021). Besides providing qualitatively different graph structure, the SBM connects our construction to projective dyadic-independence models studied within the exponential random-graph model framework of Shalizi and Rinaldo (2013). Both follow the graphon construction

Ui\displaystyle U_{i} ∼iid​Unif​(0,1),\displaystyle\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathrm{Unif}(0,1), (37)
Ai​j|Ui,Uj\displaystyle A_{ij}|U_{i},U_{j} ∼Bernoulli⁡(W⁡(Ui,Uj)),\displaystyle\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(W(U_{i},U_{j})), (38)

where W:[0,1]2→[0,1]W:[0,1]^{2}\rightarrow[0,1] maps pairs of latent positions to edge probabilities. For the exponential-decay graphon, this mapping depends directly on the distance between latent positions,

Wexp​(Ui,Uj)=exp⁡(−β​|Ui−Uj|),W_{\mathrm{exp}}(U_{i},U_{j})=\exp(-\beta|U_{i}-U_{j}|), (39)

such that connectivity decreases smoothly with latent distance. For the SBM graphon, the latent space is instead partitioned into KK blocks through a mapping b:[0,1]→{1,…,K}b:[0,1]\rightarrow\{1,\ldots,K\}. Edge probabilities are then determined by the corresponding entries of an assortative block probability matrix PP, yielding the step-function graphon

WSBM​(Ui,Uj)=Pb⁡(Ui),b⁡(Uj).W_{\mathrm{SBM}}(U_{i},U_{j})=P_{b(U_{i}),b(U_{j})}. (40)

Both DGPs define balanced seven-class node-classification problems in which labels and features depend on the latent position, with

Yi|Ui\displaystyle Y_{i}\mid U_{i} ∼PY(⋅∣Ui),\displaystyle\sim P_{Y}(\,\cdot\mid U_{i}), (41)
Xi|Ui\displaystyle X_{i}\mid U_{i} ∼PX(⋅∣Ui).\displaystyle\sim P_{X}(\,\cdot\mid U_{i}). (42)

For the exponential-decay graphon, class probabilities vary smoothly over the latent space, with greater label ambiguity near transitions between neighboring classes. For the SBM graphon, class probabilities follow the block structure but vary smoothly within blocks, with greater ambiguity near block transitions.

Each node additionally receives 12 noisy continuous and binary features that are informative of the latent class structure without deterministically identifying the observed label. Feature informativeness is likewise allowed to vary with latent position, such that graph structure and node features provide complementary and imperfect information about the class.

Complete generator specifications and parameter settings are provided in Table 2. Tables 3–4 report the realized structural properties of the generated graph sequences across 2020 independent realizations.

Each projective graphon sequence comprises six graph sizes, logarithmically spaced between 500500 and 10,00010{,}000 nodes. We first generate the largest graph and construct each smaller graph as the induced subgraph on its first nn nodes, thereby yielding a nested sequence from the same underlying realization.

Appendix C Local Bootstrap

We construct bootstrap graph replicates using a non-parametric procedure adapted from the local probability estimator of Jeong and Donnat (2025), developed under an exchangeable graphon model and exploiting node similarity. The procedure preserves the observed node set, features and labels across replicates, while resampling the graph structure from smoothed edge probabilities.

For each node i∈𝒱i\in{\mathcal{V}}, we first construct a set 𝒩k​(i){\mathcal{N}}_{k}(i) of its kk most similar nodes according to a chosen node similarity metric. In the synthetic graphon experiments, where the latent coordinates UiU_{i} are known, we use Euclidean distance in latent space,

d⁡(i,j)=‖Ui−Uj‖2,i≠j.d(i,j)=\|U_{i}-U_{j}\|_{2},\qquad i\neq j. (43)

For the OOD benchmark datasets, where latent coordinates are unavailable, we instead use the open-neighborhood Jaccard similarity suggested by Jeong and Donnat (2025),

J⁡(i,j)=|𝒩⁡(i)∩𝒩⁡(j)||𝒩⁡(i)∪𝒩⁡(j)|,i≠j,J(i,j)=\frac{|{\mathcal{N}}(i)\cap{\mathcal{N}}(j)|}{|{\mathcal{N}}(i)\cup{\mathcal{N}}(j)|},\qquad i\neq j, (44)

where 𝒩⁡(i){\mathcal{N}}(i) denotes the open graph neighborhood of node ii. This criterion favors nodes with similar observed connectivity profiles, so that the selected neighbors provide local substitutes for node ii when estimating its edge probabilities.

The directed edge probability between nodes ii and jj is then estimated by averaging the observed adjacency of jj over 𝒩k​(i){\mathcal{N}}_{k}(i):

p^i​j=1|𝒩k​(i)|​∑u∈𝒩k​(i)𝐀u​j.\hat{p}_{ij}=\frac{1}{|{\mathcal{N}}_{k}(i)|}\sum_{u\in{\mathcal{N}}_{k}(i)}{\mathbf{A}}_{uj}. (45)

Thus, p^i​j\hat{p}_{ij} is the empirical fraction of nodes locally similar to ii that are adjacent to jj in the observed graph. Because this estimate is generally asymmetric, we obtain an undirected edge probability by

p^i​jsym=12​(p^i​j+p^j​i),\hat{p}^{\mathrm{sym}}_{ij}=\frac{1}{2}(\hat{p}_{ij}+\hat{p}_{ji}), (46)

which preserves the asymptotic unbiasedness of the local probability estimator under the conditions of Jeong and Donnat (2025).

Conditional on the resulting probability matrix, bootstrap graphs are generated independently by sampling each unordered node pair according to

Ai​j,bboot|p^i​jsym​∼iid​Bernoulli​(p^i​jsym),i<j,b∈{1,…,B},A^{\mathrm{boot}}_{ij,b}|\hat{p}_{ij}^{\mathrm{sym}}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\mathrm{Bernoulli}(\hat{p}^{\mathrm{sym}}_{ij}),\qquad i<j,\quad b\in\{1,\ldots,B\}, (47)

and setting Ai​i,bboot=0A_{ii,b}^{\mathrm{boot}}=0. The complete graph resampling procedure is given in Algorithm 1. Following the finite-sample specification of Jeong and Donnat (2025), we use k=20k=20 for both the synthetic graphons and the node classification benchmark datasets.

The statistics of 2525 bootstrap graphs are compared with those of the original graphs for the synthetic graphons and node classification benchmark datasets in Tables 3– 4 and 5, respectively.

Appendix D Model Architectures and Parameters

D.1 Graph EDL Models

For the graph EDL baselines, we consider S-BGCN-K and S-BGCN-T-K (Zhao et al., 2020), GPN (Stadler et al., 2021), GPN-GDEVI and GPN-GDLAT (Hart et al., 2023), GPN-LOP (Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024b), and CUQ-GCN, CUQ-GAT, and CUQ-APPNP (Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024a). Unless otherwise specified, we use the same hyperparameters across the graphon information-growth experiments, while for the OOD benchmarks we use the dataset-specific configurations suggested in the original implementations.

GPN, GPN-GD, GPN-LOP, CUQ-GNN. GPN, all GPN-GD variants, GPN-LOP, and all CUQ-GNN variants use a learning rate of 0.010.01 across all datasets and 1010 radial-flow layers for density estimation. For GPN, all GPN-GD variants, GPN-LOP, and CUQ-APPNP, APPNP propagation uses K=10K=10. CUQ-GCN, CUQ-GAT, and CUQ-APPNP differ only in the graph convolution used before density estimation; CUQ-GAT uses one attention head per layer, negative slope 0.20.2, and no attention-coefficient dropout. GPN-GD uses the same hyperparameters as GPN, and additionally tunes the graph distance regularization weight and activation function, using the same hyperparameters for both variants. Graphon and OOD dataset-specific hyperparameters are reported in Tables 6 and 7.

S-BGCN. We evaluate S-BGCN-K and S-BGCN-T-K. We use a learning rate of 0.010.01 across datasets. S-BGCN-K uses λ1\lambda_{1} to weight the KL regularization term, while S-BGCN-T-K additionally uses λ2\lambda_{2} to weight the teacher regularization term. The graphon and OOD dataset-specific hyperparameters are reported in Table 8. Uncertainty estimates are computed using 100100 MC dropout samples.

D.2 G-Ens and GB-Ens

Unless otherwise specified, G-Ens and GB-Ens use the same hyperparameters for the graphons, while for the OOD benchmarks we perform the same dataset-specific hyperparameter search, selecting model and training hyperparameters by validation accuracy; GB-Ens additionally applies graph bootstrapping.

APPNP backbone. For the graphon experiments, we use an APPNP architecture (Gasteiger et al., 2019) consisting of a two-layer MLP with hidden dimension 6464, dropout 0.30.3, followed by APPNP propagation with K=10K=10 iterations and teleport probability α=0.1\alpha=0.1. We use a learning rate of 0.010.01 and weight decay 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}. For the OOD datasets, we fix the MLP to two layers and K=10K=10, and search over hidden dimensions in {64,128,256}\{64,128,256\}; dropout rates in {0.3,0.5,0.6}\{0.3,0.5,0.6\}; teleport probabilities in {0.05,0.1,0.2}\{0.05,0.1,0.2\}; learning rates in {0.005,0.01,0.02}\{0.005,0.01,0.02\}; and weight decay in {10−5,5×10−4,5×10−3}\{10^{-5},5\times 10^{-4},5\times 10^{-3}\}.

GAT backbone. For the graphon experiments, we use a two-layer GAT (Veličković et al., 2018) with total hidden dimension 6464, 88 attention heads, feature and attention-coefficient dropout rates of 0.30.3 and 0.20.2, respectively, attention negative slope of 0.20.2, learning rate of 0.0050.005, and weight decay of 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}. For the OOD datasets, we search over 22 or 33 GAT layers; total hidden dimensions in {64,128,256}\{64,128,256\}; 44 or 88 attention heads; feature dropout rates in {0.2,0.3,0.5,0.6}\{0.2,0.3,0.5,0.6\}; attention-coefficient dropout rates in {0.3,0.5,0.6}\{0.3,0.5,0.6\}; learning rates in {0.005,0.01}\{0.005,0.01\}; and weight decay in {10−4,10−3}\{10^{-4},10^{-3}\}. The attention negative slope is fixed to 0.20.2.

GCN backbone. For the graphon experiments, we use a two-layer GCN (Kipf and Welling, 2017) with hidden dimension 6464, dropout of 0.30.3, learning rate of 0.010.01, and weight decay of 5×10−45\times 10^{-4}. For the OOD datasets, we search over 22 or 33 GCN layers; hidden dimensions in {64,128,256}\{64,128,256\}; dropout rates in {0.2,0.4,0.5}\{0.2,0.4,0.5\}; learning rates in {0.01,0.02,0.03}\{0.01,0.02,0.03\}; and weight decay in {5×10−5,5×10−4,5×10−3}\{5\times 10^{-5},5\times 10^{-4},5\times 10^{-3}\}.

Appendix E Additional Experimental Results

RQ2: Graph EDL models are inconsistent epistemic predictors.

The SBM results in Figures 4(a) and 4(b) reproduce the patterns observed for the exponential-decay graphon: EDL methods fail to exhibit consistent EU concentration, while AU remains sensitive to the regularization parameter λ\lambda. Similar differences in EU magnitude across methods persist on real-world datasets, as shown in Table 9. For completeness, Table 10 reports predictive accuracy averaged over the two graphon sequences; GPN variants share a common parameterization, as in their original formulations, resulting in lower accuracy for some variants, particularly GPN-GDEVI.

RQ3: GB-Ens is a family of candidate consistent epistemic predictors.

Complementing the results reported in the main text, Figure 5(a) shows that on the SBM, GB-Ens EU decreases from N=500N=500 to N=10,000N=10,000 by 92%92\% for APPNP and 94%94\% for GCN, while GAT exhibits a weaker, non-monotonic EU reduction of 34%34\%, reaching a maximum of 42%42\% at an intermediate graph size. Figure 5(b) further decomposes EU into seed and bootstrap contributions of similar magnitude, both decreasing with increasing information. For GAT, the non-monotonicity is driven primarily by the seed component, whereas the bootstrap component follows a more consistently decreasing trajectory. Regarding aleatoric uncertainty, Figure 6(b) shows that GB-Ens AU decreases and eventually stabilizes, with all three backbones approaching similar plateaus.

Figure 6(a) shows that G-Ens similarly exhibit no consistent EU contraction on the SBM, while Figure 6(b) shows strongly backbone-dependent AU trajectories. For completeness, Table 12 reports predictive accuracy averaged over the two graphon information-growth sequences for G-Ens and GB-Ens. For the true-DGP resampling diagnostic, we compute normalized node-wise Wasserstein-1 distances on a random 10%10\% subset of test nodes and average them across nodes and 2020 projective-sequence replicates, using the Euclidean diameter 2\sqrt{2} of the probability simplex for normalization. Table 11 shows that, on the SBM, distances remain relatively low for GCN (0.120.12–0.140.14) and APPNP (0.200.20–0.340.34), whereas GAT exhibits larger distances ranging from 0.240.24 to 0.450.45.

Appendix F Out-Of-Distribution Detection

We report the full OOD detection results for the EDL baselines and, for completeness, extend the evaluation to G-Ens and GB-Ens in Tables 13 to 20, for which we similarly find that the most effective uncertainty type depends on the model and OOD protocol. Bold highlights the best-performing uncertainty type(s) for each model and shift. GB-Ens bootstrap and original dataset statistics are reported in Table 5. The observed discrepancies in graph statistics indicate that the local bootstrap does not preserve all topological properties of the observed graphs, limiting its fidelity as an approximation of graph observation variability; nevertheless, in these downstream OOD experiments uncertainty serves only as a detection score, and this structural degradation does not automatically translate into degraded OOD detection performance. We follow the leave-out-classes (LOC) and feature isolation (FI) protocols of Stadler et al. (2021); Damke and Hüllermeier (2024b); Damke and Hüllermeier (2024a).

On OGBN-ArXiv, CUQ-GAT and CUQ-GCN achieve very low accuracy (≈0.051\approx 0.051–0.0730.073) using the hyperparameters recommended in the original paper (Damke and Hüllermeier, 2024a), while GPN-LOP exceeds the available 80 GB of NVIDIA A100 GPU memory; we therefore do not report results for these models.

Datasets. We use CoraML (McCallum et al., 2000), CiteSeer (Giles et al., 1998), PubMed (Namata et al., 2012), CoauthorCS, CoauthorPhysics, AmazonComputers, AmazonPhotos (Shchur et al., 2018), and OGBN-ArXiv (Hu et al., 2020).

Leave-out-classes (LOC). Following Stadler et al. (2021), we partition the label space 𝒴{\mathcal{Y}} into retained classes 𝒴ID{\mathcal{Y}}_{\mathrm{ID}} and the same left-out classes 𝒴OOD{\mathcal{Y}}_{\mathrm{OOD}} used in their LOC setup. Nodes from 𝒴OOD{\mathcal{Y}}_{\mathrm{OOD}} are excluded from training and validation but remain in 𝒢{\mathcal{G}}, preserving the transductive setting. For GB-Ens, the same class partition is fixed across bootstrap replicates, with each ensemble member evaluated on its corresponding bootstrap graph.

Feature isolation (FI). We sample niso=100n_{\mathrm{iso}}=100 test nodes and, for each node ii, construct a copy of 𝒢{\mathcal{G}} in which only XiX_{i} is replaced by coordinate-wise Gaussian 𝒩⁡(0,σ2​ID){\mathcal{N}}(0,\sigma^{2}I_{D}) or Bernoulli Bernoulli⁡(0.5)\mathrm{Bernoulli}(0.5) noise. For GB-Ens, the same nodes and feature perturbations are used across bootstrap replicates. Each perturbed node is evaluated in its corresponding graph as OOD; for GB-Ens, this evaluation is performed separately on each member’s bootstrap graph, while the unperturbed test set 𝒯(te){\mathcal{T}}^{(\mathrm{te})} forms the ID set.

Metrics. Using total, aleatoric, and epistemic uncertainty as OOD scores, we report AUROC, together with ID accuracy and FI OOD accuracy.

Appendix G Computational Complexity

Graph EDL methods can themselves incur substantial computational costs, with different methods trading off preprocessing, training, inference, and memory requirements. Ensemble-based methods require repeated model fitting, but retain manageable per-model computation and peak memory and are naturally parallelizable. GPN and CUQ-GCN admit O⁡(N+M)O(N+M) implementations, whereas GPN-LOP and S-BGCN-K can incur O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) computation due to dense propagation and pairwise GKDE prior construction, respectively. For GCN-based ensembles, training costs O⁡(N+M)O(N+M) per member; GB-Ens additionally requires bootstrap generation, whose cost depends on the kk-NN construction and can reach O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) for general similarity search, although cheaper alternatives are available, such as the open Jaccard similarity metric used in our experiments. Bootstrap generation is repeated for each bootstrap sample. Across ensemble members, training cost scales linearly for both GB-Ens and G-Ens but is naturally parallelizable. Moreover, processing members independently and accumulating uncertainty statistics online keeps peak memory at O⁡(N+M)O(N+M), comparable to GPN, CUQ-GNN, and S-BGCN-K, whereas GPN-LOP can require O⁡(N2)O(N^{2}) memory due to dense propagation.

Tables 21, 22 and  23 complement the asymptotic analysis with empirical measurements on CoraML, CoauthorPhysics and OGBN-ArXiv, obtained on a dedicated NVIDIA A100 64 GB GPU. GB-Ens uses 100 models in the 25×425\times 4 bootstrap–seed decomposition, while G-Ens uses 10 randomly initialized models. Preprocessing time reports the total preprocessing cost required by each method, including generation of all bootstrap samples for GB-Ens. Epoch time is reported per model and training epoch, while inference time reports the total cost of producing one uncertainty estimate, aggregating the 100 forward passes required by GB-Ens and S-BGCN variants and the 10 forward passes required by G-Ens. Peak inference memory is measured when processing ensemble members sequentially. GB-Ens therefore trades increased total preprocessing, training, and inference costs for moderate peak memory requirements: graph bootstrapping becomes particularly costly on larger graphs, while its 100 members can be trained independently and in parallel, and sequential inference limits peak memory. This trade-off differs across EDL baselines: some avoid repeated model fitting and inference, whereas preprocessing-heavy methods such as S-BGCN-K incur comparable preprocessing costs on OGBN-ArXiv, and dense propagation makes GPN-LOP considerably more expensive on CoauthorPhysics and infeasible on OGBN-ArXiv under the available GPU memory.
